papers.title: Resist-free shadow deposition using silicon trenches for Josephson junctions in superconducting qubits
papers.abstract: Superconducting qubit fabrication innovations continue to be explored to achieve higher performance. Despite improvements to base layer fabrication and processing, resist-based Josephson junction (JJ) schemes have largely remained unchanged. The polymer mask during deposition causes chemical contamination and limits in situ and ex situ surface preparation, junction materials, and scalability. Here, we demonstrate a resist-free approach to junction fabrication based on etched silicon trenches that is CMOS compatible and easily integrated into existing innovations in qubit base layer fabrication and chemical processing. We fabricate Al-AlOx-Al JJs and qubits using this method, measuring median energy relaxation times up to 184 microseconds. We find minimal contamination at the substrate-metal interface and fluctuations of energy relaxation on a 35 hour timescale that are narrow and normally distributed. The method widens the process window for substrate preparation and new materials platforms.

similar_to.title: High coherence fluxonium manufactured with a wafer-scale uniformity process
2D transmons with lifetimes and coherence times exceeding 1 millisecond

summary.summary: A resist-free Josephson junction fabrication method based on etched silicon trenches enables Al-AlO$_x$-Al junctions without polymer contamination, producing qubits with median $T_1 = 184$ µs, median $Q_1 = 3.26$ million, and exceptionally stable coherence fluctuations over 36 hours. STEM/EELS confirms minimal carbon and oxygen contamination at the metal-substrate interface, with the process offering CMOS compatibility and broad material flexibility for future qubit platforms.
summary.motivation: Conventional resist-based Josephson junction fabrication has remained largely unchanged for 25 years despite improvements to superconductor base layers; the polymer mask causes chemical contamination and limits surface preparation, junction materials, and process scalability.
summary.method: Silicon substrates are etched with trenches using CMOS-compatible dry-etch processes; Al electrodes are deposited at $\ \pm 49°$ angles with intermediate oxidation ($1$ Torr, $5$ min, $100\%$ O$_2$) to form overlapping junctions within the trenched geometry, followed by photolithography and wet-etch patterning to define qubits.
summary.result: Five qubits with $20$–$150$ µm capacitor gaps achieve relaxation times of $14$–$185$ µs and quality factors up to $3.26$ million; $T_1$ fluctuations over $36$ hours follow Gaussian distributions with robust coefficient of variation $\leq 0.19$ (significantly lower than comparable resist-based devices), and Allan deviation analysis shows $\sigma_{T_1} \approx 7.5$ µs, compared to $\approx 13$ µs for similar-performance resist-based junctions.

papers.title: First-principles study of dispersive readout in circuit QED
papers.abstract: The speed and fidelity of dispersive readout of superconducting qubits should improve by increasing the amplitude of the measurement drive. Experiments show, however, that beyond some drive amplitude there is always a saturation or drop in fidelity, often associated with a decrease in qubit energy relaxation time $T_1$. A simple Lindblad master equation does not capture the latter effect. More involved approaches based on effective master equations rely on strong assumptions about the spectra of the system and the bath and only partially agree with observations. Here, we perform a first-principles simulation of the full unitary dynamics of dispersive readout by considering the circuit QED Hamiltonian coupled to a microscopic model for the measurement transmission line, allowing for its arbitrary spectrum, including filters. Our access to the dynamics of the bath degrees of freedom allows us to investigate the emission spectrum of the system as a function of drive power. We show how the dependence of qubit $T_1$ on readout drive amplitude is sensitive to the details of the bath spectrum. In particular, we find that $T_1$ drops with increasing drive amplitude when a Purcell notch filter is placed at the qubit frequency, and that the Lindblad master equation shows general qualitative defects compared to the first-principles model.

similar_to.title: Enhancing Dispersive Readout of Superconducting Qubits Through Dynamic Control of the Dispersive Shift: Experiment and Theory
Realizing Rapid, High-Fidelity, Single-Shot Dispersive Readout of Superconducting Qubits

summary.summary: A first-principles tensor-network simulation of circuit QED dispersive readout captures the full unitary dynamics of a qubit and resonator coupled to a microscopic bath with arbitrary spectral density, avoiding standard Lindblad approximations. The study reveals that the qubit energy relaxation time $T_1$ can either decrease or increase with readout drive amplitude ($n̄$ photons) depending sensitively on the bath spectral function, with a Purcell notch filter at $ω_q$ producing qualitatively different behavior ($T_1$ increases with $n̄$) than Ohmic or flat spectra, contradicting predictions from simple Lindblad master equations.
summary.motivation: Dispersive readout fidelity in superconducting qubits saturates or drops beyond certain drive amplitudes, accompanied by unexpected changes in $T_1$—a phenomenon not captured by standard phenomenological master equations. Understanding this effect requires a microscopic model of the measurement transmission line's frequency-dependent coupling to the system.
summary.method: The authors simulate the time evolution of the circuit QED Hamiltonian (qubit at $ω_q/2π = 5.304$ GHz, resonator at $ω_a/2π = 7.5$ GHz, coupling $g/2π = 0.3165$ GHz) linearly coupled to a bath described by spectral density $J(ω)$, using tensor-network time-dependent variational principle (TDVP) with matrix-product states to evolve the full wavefunction. They extract qubit relaxation rates $Γ_{10}(n̄)$ by fitting exponential decay of $⟨Σ_z(t)⟩$ and reconstruct bath mode occupations $⟨n̂_ω⟩$ to perform frequency-resolved spectroscopy.
summary.result: For an Ohmic spectrum with $J(ω) ∝ ω$ and Purcell filter depth $D = 0.7$, $σ = 0.1$ at $ω_q$, the normalized relaxation rate $Γ_{10}(n̄)/Γ_{10}(0)$ increases monotonically with photon number when the filter suppresses $J(ω_q)$, whereas for unfiltered Ohmic and flat spectra it decreases. The Lindblad model (Eq. 7) with single-photon dissipator predicts only monotonic decrease, failing qualitatively in the filtered case; agreement with microscopic Fermi's Golden Rule predictions (Eq. 22) confirms the importance of counter-rotating terms and spectral function evaluation at $ω_q$ rather than $ω_a$.

papers.title: Multiplexed cryo-CMOS control of an isolated double quantum dot
papers.abstract: Scalable spin-based quantum computing demands precise and stable control of a large number of gate-defined quantum dots while minimizing wiring complexity and thermal load. Control architectures based on sample-and-hold (SH) multiplexing techniques offer a promising solution by enabling sequential programming of several gate voltages using a limited number of input lines. However, the compatibility of such dynamic voltage refreshing with the stringent stability, noise, and speed requirements of quantum dot operation is an active subject of study. Here we experimentally demonstrate that a multiplexing cryo-CMOS circuit can reliably bias a silicon double quantum dot (DQD) at 0.5K. Exploiting the isolated regime, we show deterministic loading and isolation of four electrons and stable access to all five charge configurations from (4,0) to (0,4), despite the sequential voltage refreshing. We further demonstrate rapid voltage pulsing across an inter-dot transition, resolving single-electron tunneling events and stochastic switching at the (1,3)-(0,4) transition. These results confirm that SH-based multiplexed control is compatible with both static biasing and pulsing of isolated quantum dots, representing an important milestone toward scalable cryogenic control architectures for large-scale spin-qubit processors.

similar_to.title: A digitally controlled silicon quantum processing unit
Superconducting Flux Memory for Cryogenic Applications

summary.summary: A cryo-CMOS sample-and-hold multiplexing circuit successfully controls a silicon double quantum dot at 0.5 K, demonstrating stable biasing of all five charge configurations from $(4,0)$ to $(0,4)$ and rapid voltage pulsing that resolves single-electron tunneling events. This validates that SH-based multiplexed control is compatible with both static and dynamic operation of isolated quantum dots, advancing scalable architectures for large-scale spin-qubit processors.
summary.motivation: Scaling gate-defined spin qubits to millions requires reducing wiring complexity and thermal load from the cryostat while maintaining precise voltage control; sample-and-hold multiplexing offers a solution but its compatibility with stringent quantum dot stability and pulsing requirements remained experimentally unvalidated.
summary.method: A cryo-CMOS demultiplexer biasing seven gates of a FDSOI silicon DQD at 0.5 K sequentially refreshes voltages using two analog inputs with 6.4 µs per refresh cycle; charge stability is mapped via RF-SET reflectometry ($91.5\%$ fidelity between $(0,4)$ and $(1,3)$) and pulsing dynamics are captured in single-shot readout traces.
summary.result: Voltage drift measured at $1.5$ V is $5.5$ µV with exponential dependence on voltage, allowing projection of biasing $>10^7$ independent gates at $<100$ µV error from one input; inter-dot charge transitions show well-defined four parallel lines despite sequential refreshing, and pulsing resolves stochastic tunneling events at the $(1,3)$–$(0,4)$ transition with response time faster than the $\sim 1$ ms inter-dot tunnel coupling.

papers.title: Logical Compilation for Multi-Qubit Iceberg Patches
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in quantum computing have enabled practical use of quantum error detecting and correcting codes. However, current architectures and future proposals of quantum computer design suffer from limited qubit counts, necessitating the use of high-rate codes. Such codes, with their code parameters denoted as $[[n, k, d]]$, have more than $1$ logical qubit per code (i.e., $k > 1$). This leads to reduced error tolerance of the code, since $\lceil (d-1)/2\rceil$ errors on any of the $n$ physical qubits can affect the logical state of all $k$ logical qubits. Therefore, it becomes critical to optimally map the input qubits of a quantum circuit to these codes, in such a way that the circuit fidelity is maximized. \par However, the problem of mapping program qubits to logical qubits for high-rate codes has not been studied in prior work. A brute force search to find the optimal mapping is super exponential (scaling as $O(n!)$, where $n$ is the number of input qubits), making exhaustive search infeasible past a small number of qubits. We propose a framework that addresses this problem on two fronts: (1) for any given mapping, it performs logical-to-physical compilation that translates input gates into efficiently encoded implementations utilizing Hadamard commutation and gate merging; and (2) it quickly searches the space of possible mappings through a merge-optimizing, noise-biased packing heuristic that identifies high-performing qubit assignments without exhaustive enumeration. To the best of our knowledge, our compiler is the first work to explore mapping and compilation for high-rate codes. Across 71 benchmark circuits, we reduce circuit depth by $34\%$, gate counts by up to $31\%$ and $17\%$ for one-qubit and two-qubit gates, and improve total variation distance by $1.75\times$, with logical selection rate improvements averaging $86\%$ relative to naive compilation.

similar_to.title: Suppressing quantum errors by scaling a surface code logical qubit
High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory

summary.summary: This paper addresses the problem of mapping program qubits to logical qubits in high-rate quantum error detection codes, specifically the $[[4,2,2]]$ Iceberg code which encodes two logical qubits per patch. The authors present a compilation framework combining Hadamard commutation, gate merging, and noise-biased packing heuristics that reduces circuit depth by 34%, gate counts by 31% and 17% for one- and two-qubit gates respectively, and improves logical selection rate by 86% relative to naive compilation.
summary.motivation: Current quantum error detecting/correcting architectures require high-rate codes with $k > 1$ logical qubits per patch due to limited physical qubit counts, but the optimal assignment of program qubits to these patches has not been previously studied, creating a critical gap in compilation techniques as codes with multiple logical qubits reduce error tolerance and make qubit placement decisions material to circuit fidelity.
summary.method: The framework performs Hadamard commutation to reduce expensive single-qubit gates, executes gate merging to combine compatible operations into cheaper transversal or patch-wise implementations, and employs a greedy packing heuristic with noise-biased scoring (weighting merge savings, delay penalties, and gate-type preferences) to solve the qubit assignment problem in $O(n^2 \cdot m \log m)$ time, avoiding the $O(n!)$ brute-force search.
summary.result: Across 71 QASMBench circuits up to 150 logical qubits, the framework achieves average reductions of 31% in single-qubit gates, 17% in two-qubit gates, 34% in depth, improves total variation distance by 1.75$\times$, and logical selection rate by 86%, with gains remaining stable as circuits scale and greatest improvements at tight packing density ($n/k = 2$).
